investigations.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids – II
investigations.objective: Study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flow in microgravity, and begin to bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 and real material flammability in microgravity.
investigations.resultSummary: About 130 flame tests on PMMA films, slabs, rods, fabrics and a candle in a small wind tunnel on the ISS, with O2 reduced below 21 % by nitrogen dilution. Flames were very sensitive to air flow between 0 and 5 cm/s and could survive at flows below 1 cm/s as dim blue flames that flare up when flow increases. Measured heat-release rates were mostly below 100 W.
investigations.earthRelevance: Validated combustion models apply to wildfires, building fires and waste-to-energy combustion (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Burning and Suppression of Solids
investigations.objective: Bridge the gap between the 1-g NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, ground-based microgravity tests and real material flammability in microgravity, and assess how well an inert gaseous extinguishing agent (N2, similar to that used on ISS) puts out flames.
investigations.resultSummary: Over a hundred small-scale ISS tests burned fabrics, PMMA spheres and slabs and candles in a low-speed air flow, sometimes followed by an N2 jet to try to extinguish them. Flames were especially sensitive to flow in the 0–5 cm/s range; at the lowest flows they became dim and blue but could keep burning for a long time.
investigations.earthRelevance: Microgravity-validated combustion models feed back into terrestrial fire models (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Safety Experiment – I
investigations.objective: Determine how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity and compare low-g flammability limits with NASA's 1-g material screening test.
investigations.resultSummary: The first intentionally large fire set inside an orbiting spacecraft: a 94 x 40.6 cm cotton-fiberglass sheet burned in a 20 cm/s air flow, once with and once against the flow. In concurrent spread the flame size stayed limited after ignition, unlike the accelerating upward fire seen on Earth.
investigations.earthRelevance: Fire behaviour in small sealed volumes informs fire safety in mines, aircraft and submarines (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment – II
investigations.objective: Measure low-g flammability of several spacecraft materials at realistic scale and compare with NASA's 1-g material flammability screening test.
investigations.resultSummary: Nine material samples were burned one after another in a Cygnus vehicle. Thin silicone did not sustain a flame in microgravity, while cotton-fiberglass fabric burned its full 29 cm length at 2.1–2.6 mm/s. Thick PMMA flames stayed anchored near the base, spreading far more slowly than the 1-g comparison.
investigations.earthRelevance: Low-pressure ground tests may approximate untested gravity levels for thick and thin solids (NTRS 20200000557).

investigations.name: Spacecraft Fire Experiment – III
investigations.objective: Repeat the Saffire-I large-scale fabric burn at a higher flow (30 cm/s) to see how rapidly a large fire grows in low gravity and whether it reaches a steady spread rate.
investigations.resultSummary: Two large SIBAL sheets were burned in a Cygnus vehicle at 30 cm/s air flow (one concurrent, one opposed), extending Saffire-I's 20 cm/s case. The PSI table lists conditions only; no burn results are tabulated.
investigations.earthRelevance: Fire behaviour in sealed vehicles informs fire safety in mines, aircraft and submarines (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment
investigations.objective: Map flammability limits of liquid fuels in microgravity, measure the effectiveness of gaseous suppressants (CO2, He) and determine the limiting oxygen index (LOI) as a function of pressure and suppressant concentration.
investigations.resultSummary: 274 droplet tests burned methanol and heptane in mixtures of O2, N2, CO2 and He at 0.7–3 atm. Each test ended in flame extinction, droplet disruption or burning to completion. The data give the oxygen level below which these fuels stop burning and how much CO2 or helium is needed.
investigations.earthRelevance: Suppressant effectiveness results can inform less harmful fire-suppression systems; relevant to submarines and high-altitude aircraft (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Flame Extinguishment Experiment – 2
investigations.objective: Extend FLEX to fuels and conditions closer to real combustors: bi-component droplets, soot formation, extinction boundaries, droplet arrays and slow convective flow, to provide benchmark data for numerical models.
investigations.resultSummary: FLEX-2 burned single and paired droplets of pure fuels and mixtures in O2/N2 and O2/He atmospheres at 0.5–3 atm to provide benchmark data for droplet combustion models. PSI publishes only the planned test matrix, not per-test results.
investigations.earthRelevance: Benchmark droplet data support surrogate fuels and cleaner, more efficient combustor and jet-engine design (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Cool Flames Investigation
investigations.objective: Study low-temperature 'cool flame' droplet combustion of n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures at 0.5–5 atm, including helium dilution, and relate droplet size, pressure and extinction.
investigations.resultSummary: 79 unique droplet tests explored how dodecane droplets keep burning after the visible hot flame goes out, sustained by an invisible low-temperature 'cool flame'. Hot- and cool-flame burning rates and extinction diameters are tabulated for most tests.
investigations.earthRelevance: Cool-flame chemistry matters for ignition of practical fuels and for HCCI / diesel engine design (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment
investigations.objective: Measure the size of smoke particles produced by overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity and relate them to smoke generation and transport, to evaluate and design spacecraft smoke detectors.
investigations.resultSummary: Spacecraft materials were overheated on the ISS to produce smoke, which was aged and measured by detectors and particle samplers. The hypothesis was that low-gravity smoke particles grow larger than on Earth, which could change how smoke detectors respond.
investigations.earthRelevance: Better smoke detectors for extreme environments such as submarines and underwater laboratories (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment – Reflight
investigations.objective: Repeat SAME with new materials (Pyrell foam), wider conditions (higher heating, no-flow heating) and better diagnostics to quantify smoke particle size distributions in low gravity.
investigations.resultSummary: SAME-R completed 66 test points on the ISS in July–September 2010 with five spacecraft materials. Most average smoke particle sizes were 200–400 nm, with some quiescent (no-flow) cases producing substantially larger particles.
investigations.earthRelevance: Detector designs from SAME data apply to submarines and underwater laboratories (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: ACME – Burning Rate Emulator
investigations.objective: Use a gas burner that emulates condensed (solid/liquid) fuels to find the conditions for steady burning in a quiescent microgravity ambient, including candidate spacecraft atmospheres (21 % O2 at 14.7 psia, 26.5 % at 10.2 psia, 34 % at 8.2 psia).
investigations.resultSummary: A gas-fed burner emulating solids like PMMA and nylon burned in still air on the ISS. In elevated-oxygen atmospheres being considered for future spacecraft the flames kept burning without any air flow, whereas at 21 % O2 they self-extinguished in a short time.
investigations.earthRelevance: Links microgravity flammability to cone-calorimeter (NASA-STD-6001 Test 2) material properties (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: ACME – Cool Flames Investigation with Gases
investigations.objective: Determine the conditions for steady cool diffusion flames of gaseous fuels on spherical porous burners, for normal and inverse flames over a broad range of stoichiometric mixture fraction, adiabatic flame temperature and flow rate.
investigations.resultSummary: Spherical gas flames on the ISS were used to look for cool flames and to map when flames ignite, self-extinguish or burn until the fuel is cut. Inverse flames reached the highest oxygen levels flown in these data (oxidizer stream up to 85 % O2), but they are gas flames, not burning materials.
investigations.earthRelevance: Cool-flame kinetics could enable ultra-lean, higher-efficiency engines (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: ACME – Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames
investigations.objective: Understand how electric fields act on laminar diffusion flames in microgravity: voltage vs chemi-ion current, dynamic flame response, soot formation and stabilized near-limit lifted flames.
investigations.resultSummary: Methane and ethylene flames on the ISS were exposed to electric fields of either polarity to study ion-driven flows, soot and flame stability without buoyancy. It is a fundamental combustion study, not a fire-safety test.
investigations.earthRelevance: Electric-field flame control may lower soot and pollutant emissions and improve combustion efficiency (PSI research impacts).

investigations.name: Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment
investigations.objective: Find the laminar smoke point (onset of soot emission) of non-buoyant gas-jet flames in co-flowing air and how burner diameter, co-flow velocity and fuel affect it.
investigations.resultSummary: 526 small gas-jet flames were studied in the glovebox to find when they begin to emit soot. Soot governs flame heat emission, so the data help predict fire spread and support material flammability criteria.
investigations.earthRelevance: Better soot control for jet engines and power-generation boilers (NTRS 20090014827).

investigations.name: Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment
investigations.objective: Understand the structure and stability (lift-off, blow-out) of laminar co-flow diffusion flames in microgravity, including fuel dilution effects on soot.
investigations.resultSummary: On 12 test days in 2012, methane, ethylene and other gas flames were photographed in co-flowing air to study lift-off, blow-out and soot. Microgravity flames were longer and sootier than their 1-g counterparts.
investigations.earthRelevance: Improved soot and flame-stability models for cleaner engines and industrial burners (PSI research impacts).

missions.notes: Sea-level air: NASA's OCHMO technical brief states the ISS cabin is 'typically maintained at 14.7 psia with 21% O2' (14.7 psia = 101.3 kPa). history.title: Apollo 1 pad fire
history.summary: During a preflight test of Apollo 204 (AS-204), a fire swept through the command module and killed Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee. NASA then sharply limited the amount and location of combustible materials in the command module and flight suits, pursued fire-resistant fabrics such as PBI, and changed ground procedures from 100% O2 to a 60% O2 / 40% N2 mixture.
history.quote: Astronauts Virgil Grissom, Edward White and Roger Chaffee lost their lives when a fire swept through the command module.
history.lesson: Oxygen-rich cabin atmospheres plus flammable materials are the core risk EMBER's oxygen-limit evidence addresses.

history.title: Apollo 13 oxygen tank failure
history.summary: Oxygen tank no. 2 in the service module failed from combustion inside the tank. The Apollo 13 Review Board found the most probable cause was ignition of Teflon wire insulation on the fan motor wires by electric arcs; the insulation had been damaged when heater thermostatic switches failed closed during ground detanking. It showed that materials normally thought safe can burn in pure, high-pressure oxygen.
history.quote: The cause of the combustion was most probably the ignition of Teflon wire insulation on the fan motor wires, caused by electric arcs in this wiring.
history.lesson: Ignition sources and materials in oxygen systems need flammability testing at the real oxygen condition.

history.title: Fire aboard space station Mir (oxygen candle)
history.summary: With six crew aboard, a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister (lithium perchlorate 'candle') in Mir's Kvant-1 module ignited and shot a flame about three feet long. It blocked access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles and filled the modules with smoke. The crew put the fire out; life support cleared the smoke over several hours. Lessons were carried into ISS design and operations.
history.quote: The searing flame, lasting several minutes, not only cut off access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles but also filled the station’s modules with smoke.
history.lesson: Smoke spreads through the whole station and escape routes can be cut off, which is why detection (SAME) and suppression (FLEX) data matter. NASA dates the fire Feb. 24, 1997; some accounts give Feb. 23 (US time).

sources.label: NASA History – 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir

history.title: Saffire: setting real fires in an empty spacecraft
history.summary: Because earlier microgravity fire tests used samples of only about 10 cm, NASA ran Saffire inside uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicles after they left the ISS. Saffire-I and -III burned a large cotton-fiberglass sheet (about 0.94 m x 0.4 m) and Saffire-II burned nine Test 1-sized samples. It was the first test of spacecraft fires at a realistic scale. Results showed that the size of the enclosure around a fire matters more than expected. Saffire IV-VI followed with fires up to 10 kW.
history.quote: The Saffire Experiment represents the first test of spacecraft fires at a scale relevant to real spacecraft.
history.lesson: Fire growth does not scale linearly from small samples, so large-scale data are needed to validate material limits and fire models.

history.title: First extended burns in simulated lunar gravity (LUCI)
history.summary: The Lunar Combustion Investigation spun a Blue Origin New Shepard rocket to create lunar gravity and ran the first combustion tests longer than 25 s at lunar g, burning a cotton-fiberglass fabric and a 4 mm PMMA rod in air. It leads into FM2 (Flammability of Materials on the Moon), planned to launch in late 2026. This is the partial-gravity data PSI does not yet contain.
history.quote: These are the first-ever, extended-duration (greater than 25 seconds) combustion tests performed in simulated Lunar gravity.
history.lesson: Partial-gravity flammability is only now being measured; EMBER marks lunar and Mars answers as 1 g / 0 g bounds, not measurements.

earth.title: Lightweight firefighter air tanks (SCBA)
earth.summary: NASA Johnson Space Center and Scott Aviation developed a lighter firefighter breathing-air backpack: about 20 lb for a 30-minute supply (13 lb less than conventional tanks), pressurized at 4,500 psi, built from an aluminum liner wrapped in resin-impregnated glass fibers.
earth.quote: New backpack system weighs only 20 pounds for 30 minute air supply, 13 pounds less than conventional firefighting tanks.
earth.linkNote: Heritage spinoff from spacecraft pressure-vessel technology; not derived from a PSI combustion investigation.

earth.title: Incipient fire detector from the Space Shuttle
earth.summary: The Brunswick Incipient Fire Detector, first used in Space Shuttle orbiters, samples air for combustion particles and can tell them apart from dust, so it gives fewer false alarms and can signal a fire before flame and smoke appear. SAME and SAME-R carry this line forward: they measured how smoke particle sizes change in microgravity to set the requirements for next-generation spacecraft smoke detectors, and NASA notes the resulting detectors could also serve submarines and underwater laboratories.
earth.quote: Fire detector represents an advancement over commercially available smoke detectors in that it senses and signals the presence of a fire condition before appearance of flame and smoke.

earth.title: New technology for fire attire (Project FIRES, PBI fabric)
earth.summary: Project FIRES, sponsored by NASA and FEMA's U.S. Fire Administration and managed by Marshall Space Flight Center, applied lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials developed for spacesuits and spacecraft to firefighter turnout gear. After the Apollo 1 fire NASA pushed PBI fiber for flight suits; PBI later became the PBI Gold outer shell used in firefighter gear. This is the same material-flammability question BASS, BASS-II and Saffire study in microgravity.
earth.quote: A major focus of the effort involves application to the FIRES ensemble of lightweight, fire-resistant, heat-protective materials originally developed for use in astronauts' space suits or in spacecraft components which require thermal protection.
earth.linkNote: Thematic link (material flammability), not a direct technology transfer from these experiments.

earth.title: Fine-water-mist fire extinguisher
earth.summary: NASA Glenn and ADA Technologies (SBIR funding over about 10 years) built a fine-water-mist portable extinguisher for the ISS to replace CO2 units: 6 lb of water and 1.2 lb of nitrogen, working in any orientation. Its zero-leak valve maker (Doering) now sells the same class of valve to industry. FLEX measured how gaseous suppressants (CO2, He) and exploration atmospheres affect extinction in microgravity, the evidence base for choosing spacecraft suppressants.
earth.quote: A fine-water-mist portable fire extinguisher made the most sense: it wouldn’t cause damage to structures or require special cleanup procedures and would meet the other criteria.
earth.linkNote: FLEX studied gaseous suppressants, not water mist; the link is the shared question of what to put out a spacecraft fire with.

earth.title: Wool filters for fire respirators
earth.summary: Work to extend the life of the respirator Orion crews would wear during a cabin fire led New Zealand company Lanaco to improve its wool filter line for firefighters on Earth. NASA notes Orion crews could have to stay longer in a fire-contaminated cabin than ISS crews.
earth.quote: A New Zealand-based company’s work to help astronauts fight fires in case of an anomaly on the Orion spacecraft is already informing its line of wool filters for firefighters on Earth.

earth.summary: NASA expects that smoke detectors developed from SAME results could also be used in extreme environments on Earth such as submarines or underwater laboratories, where accurate smoke detection can save lives.

earth.title: Less harmful fire suppressants (FLEX)
earth.summary: According to NASA, FLEX findings on CO2, He and SF6 suppressant effectiveness can lead to more efficient, less harmful suppression systems and better fire safety in confined spaces such as submarines and high-altitude aircraft. Its cool-flame findings also inform engine design.
earth.quote: The mission's findings on the effectiveness of various fire suppressants, including CO2, He, and SF6, in microgravity can lead to the development of more efficient and less harmful fire suppression systems, reducing the risk of toxic byproducts during fire events.

earth.title: Better fire models for wildfires and buildings (BASS / BASS-II)
earth.summary: BASS-II helps engineers choose safer materials. Because flames in microgravity are simpler, they are used to check computer models of burning, which NASA says can then be applied to wildfires, building fires and waste-to-energy combustion.
earth.quote: These models can then be used to more accurately study flames on Earth, such as in wildfires, building fires, energy recapture from waste recycling, and other combustion problems.

extractionEval.method: Concept section 8, check 2. Claims in claims.json were produced in the LLM-extractor role (extractedBy 'llm') from cached NTRS abstracts and PSI investigation records (pipeline/content/cache/sources.json). A systematic sample of 36 (every 4th claim: c-0001, c-0005, ... c-0141) was re-checked by a separate manual-annotator pass: the cited source was re-read, a gold statement written from the source alone, and the LLM statement graded correct (fully supported, right investigation), partial (true but with an attribution, tense or quote-coverage problem) or wrong (contradicted or unsupported). Programmatic check: every quote was searched verbatim in the cached source text (whitespace/quote-mark normalized; also exact substring): 36/36 sampled and 145/145 of all claims matched (100%). Verbatim quotes do not guarantee a correct claim - all partial verdicts below have verbatim quotes. Caveats: the annotator is the same model family as the extractor (not an independent human), so agreement is likely optimistic; before this evaluation, 2 non-sampled claims from NTRS 20150018397 were re-attributed from CFI to FLEX after review.

items.goldText: Objective 1 of BASS: begin to bridge the gap between NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (1 g), ground-based microgravity tests and real microgravity flammability.
items.llmText: BASS aimed to begin bridging the gap between the normal-gravity NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 method, ground-based microgravity tests and actual material flammability in microgravity.
items.note: Matches PSI-26 objective 1.

items.goldText: PSI-26 states current spacecraft material selection uses NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which sorts materials by 1-g behavior with no consideration of low-gravity effects.
items.llmText: Current NASA spacecraft material selection (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) segregates materials on 1-g behavior without considering low-gravity effects.

items.goldText: The smallest acrylic-slab flames were hurt by conductive heat loss yet still burned >5 min before self-extinguishing; authors note a tiny flame might go undetected for a long time.
items.llmText: Even the smallest BASS flames on acrylic slabs burned for over 5 minutes before self-extinguishing, so a tiny flame might go undetected for a long time.
items.note: Faithful; the claim omits the 'conductive heat loss' qualifier but does not change the meaning.

items.goldText: BASS-II objective 1: study ignition, flame growth, spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.
items.llmText: BASS-II objective: study ignition, flame growth, flame spread and extinction limits of solid fuels in low-velocity forced flows in microgravity.

items.goldText: NASA's 1-g upward-burning test is considered the worst-case geometry on Earth but may not be conservative for flammability in space (BASS-II hypothesis section).
items.llmText: NASA's upward-burning 1-g material test is considered worst case on Earth but may not be conservative for flammability in space.
items.note: The source frames this inside the hypothesis section; claim keeps it as a statement of NASA's own concern, which is acceptable.

items.goldText: SIBAL fabric (1.2/2.2 cm x 10 cm) in low-speed concurrent flow: quenching speeds 1-5 cm/s, higher quench speed in lower O2 (21% to 16% tested). Work is part of both BASS and BASS-II.
items.llmText: For the SIBAL cotton-fiberglass fabric in concurrent flow, low-speed quenching extinction occurred at 1 to 5 cm/s, with higher quench speed at lower oxygen.
items.note: Numbers correct, but the source says the tests belong to 'the NASA BASS and BASS-II experimental projects'; attributing only to BASS-II loses half the provenance.

items.goldText: For PMMA rods in concurrent flow, the blowoff branch of the flammability boundary is linear in oxygen concentration and stretch rate.
items.llmText: On the blowoff branch the PMMA-rod flammability boundary depends linearly on oxygen concentration and stretch rate.

items.goldText: Ground (1 g) PMMA rods 0.635-3.81 cm at 14-18% O2: blowoff limits agree with BASS-II microgravity results once buoyant stretch and blockage factor are included.
items.llmText: Normal-gravity blowoff limits for PMMA rods (0.635-3.81 cm, 14-18% O2) compare favorably with BASS-II when buoyant stretch and blockage are accounted for.
items.note: Claim correctly identifies these as normal-gravity tests compared against BASS-II.

items.goldText: Saffire-I: SIBAL sample, air flow velocity 20 cm/s.
items.llmText: Saffire-I was conducted at an air flow velocity of 20 cm/s.

items.goldText: Saffire downlinked data resolved whether flame growth reaches a steady size; the enclosure size around the sample affected spread more than expected.
items.llmText: Saffire data resolved whether flame growth reaches a steady size and showed the enclosure around the sample affects flame spread more than anticipated.
items.note: Content correct, but the 2018 abstract summarizes the Saffire series, not Saffire-I alone; the inv attribution is an inference. The source sentence itself is ungrammatical ('data show resolved').

items.goldText: 2015 plan: Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 = meter-scale sample flame-spread tests in the Cygnus pressurized volume, burned to completion.
items.llmText: Saffire-1 and Saffire-3 were planned as flame spread tests of a meter-scale sample burned to completion inside the Cygnus pressurized volume.
items.note: Planned design, stated as 'planned' in the claim. Also applies to Saffire-III.

items.llmText: Saffire-II carried 9 samples of 5 cm x 29 cm: SIBAL, silicone, structural PMMA, flat PMMA and PMMA with Nomex.
items.note: Facts are in PSI-99, but the quote only supports the count and size; the material list comes from a different sentence and is not covered by the quote.

items.llmText: Pre-flight silicone samples for Saffire matched the NASA 6001 Test 1 geometry, 5 cm wide by 30 cm tall, in four thicknesses (0.25-1.00 mm).

items.goldText: Saffire-III flow was either concurrent or opposed.
items.llmText: Saffire-III flows were either concurrent or opposed to flame spread.

items.goldText: FLEX: determine LOI as a function of ambient pressure and how a suppressant changes it.
items.llmText: A primary FLEX objective was the Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) versus ambient pressure and how a suppressant changes the LOI.

items.llmText: Droplets of 1.5-4 mm were used to capture both diffusive extinction and radiative extinction.

items.goldText: FLEX-2 objective 5: influence of droplet interactions on flammability limits and extinction of droplet arrays.
items.llmText: FLEX-2 studied how droplet interactions affect flammability limits and extinction of droplet arrays.

items.goldText: SAME hypothesis: in microgravity, smoke particles from pyrolyzing/smoldering sources grow larger than in 1 g (nucleation, condensation, coagulation).
items.llmText: SAME hypothesis: without buoyant flows, smoke from a pyrolyzing source grows larger particles in microgravity than in 1g.
items.note: Correctly labelled as a hypothesis, not a result.

items.goldText: Shuttle experiments confirmed that in some cases particle sizes increase in low gravity and that ISS vs shuttle detector relative performance changes; data were insufficient to design new detectors.
items.llmText: Shuttle experiments confirmed that particle sizes can increase in low gravity and that relative ISS vs shuttle detector performance changes.
items.note: Claim omits that the size data were insufficient for detector design; meaning preserved.

items.goldText: Shuttle (ionization) and ISS (near-IR forward scattering) smoke detectors were designed without any low-gravity smoke or background-dust size data.
items.llmText: Shuttle and ISS smoke detection systems were designed without any data on low-gravity smoke or background dust size distributions.

items.goldText: SAME-R flight tests July 16 - Sept 9, 2010, 66 test points.
items.llmText: SAME-R completed 66 test points from July 16 to September 9, 2010.

items.goldText: CFI objectives: n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane at 0.25-5 atm (objective 1) and helium-dilution effects (objective 2). Approach text says chamber gas 0.25-0.5 atm.
items.llmText: CFI examined n-dodecane and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane droplets at pressures from 0.25 to 5 atm and the effect of helium dilution on cool flames.
items.note: Quote supports only objective 1; helium part comes from another line. PSI-39 is internally inconsistent on the pressure range (objective 0.25-5 atm vs approach 0.25-0.5 atm); claim reports only the objective range without flagging this.

items.goldText: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet burning was first observed on ISS in the CIR with n-alkane fuels.
items.llmText: Cool-flame-supported quasi-steady droplet combustion was first observed on ISS in the Combustion Integrated Rack with n-alkane fuels.
items.note: Statement is correct, but the first observation was made in the earlier FLEX droplet tests; attaching it to CFI implies CFI discovered cool flames.

items.goldText: BRE objective 1 plans to examine NASA-considered atmospheres 14.7 psia/21%, 10.2 psia/26.5%, 8.2 psia/34%.
items.llmText: BRE examined NASA-considered crew atmospheres: 14.7 psia / 21% O2, 10.2 psia / 26.5% O2 and 8.2 psia / 34% O2.
items.note: Source says these atmospheres 'will be examined' (planned objective). The claim's past tense implies they were tested; PSI-20 does not confirm which were actually flown.

items.llmText: BRE flight tests used CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter.
items.note: Source states an objective ('Observe ...'), not a flown test matrix; claim says 'flight tests used'. 25/50 mm burners are confirmed for drop tests in NTRS 20160010073.

items.goldText: Cool diffusion flames: peak temperature 500-1000 K; discovered in 2012.
items.llmText: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of 500-1000 K and were discovered in 2012.

items.goldText: Three ACME studies - soot processes, flame dynamics, low-temperature combustion - used porous spherical burners giving a nominally 1-D flame.
items.llmText: Three ACME studies (soot processes, flame dynamics, low-temperature combustion) used porous spherical burners for a nominally 1-D flame.
items.note: Source is the ACME overview, not CFI-G specific; CFI-G is the low-temperature study so attribution is reasonable.

items.goldText: Microgravity is ideal for isolating electric-field effects from buoyancy forces.
items.llmText: Microgravity isolates electric-field effects from buoyancy forces.

items.goldText: SPICE fuels: methane, ethylene, propane, propylene, propylene mixtures.
items.llmText: SPICE fuels included methane, ethylene, propane, propylene and propylene mixtures.

items.goldText: SLICE CH4 coflow flames: soot distribution shifts from centerline (1 g) to the wings (microgravity).
items.llmText: From normal gravity to microgravity, soot shifts from the flame centerline to the wings.

items.goldText: Flow-tunnel microgravity tests: 1g ULOI and 1g MOC are up to 4% O2 higher than 0g values, i.e. fuels burned in 0g at lower O2 than under NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
items.llmText: In microgravity flow-tunnel tests, the 1g Upward Limiting Oxygen Index and Maximum Oxygen Concentration exceeded 0g values by up to 4% O2, i.e. fuels burned in 0g at lower O2 than in NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
items.note: Not one of the 15 PSI investigations (inv = null). Source does not say the tests were in orbit (likely drop-tower); claim says 'microgravity flow-tunnel tests', which matches.

items.goldText: At 8.2 psia / 34-40% O2, material flammability is the critical hurdle: 70% of assessed subsystems need material replacements, many not yet developed.
items.llmText: In an 8.2 psia / 34-40% O2 environment, 70% of assessed ISS-heritage ECLSS subsystems would need material replacements.
